value.overview: The Pine Warbler (Setophaga pinus) is a small North American wood-warbler closely associated with pine forests. It has olive-green upperparts, yellow underparts, two white wingbars, and a relatively stout bill. Unlike many warblers, it often forages high in pine trees and regularly eats seeds as well as insects. Most of its population breeds in the southeastern United States and migrates short to moderate distances within North America.
value.classification: The Pine Warbler belongs to the family Parulidae, the wood-warblers, and the genus Setophaga. Its scientific name is Setophaga pinus.
value.identification: Adults are olive-green above and yellow below, with the yellow strongest on the throat and breast. The wings show two distinct white bars, and the tail has white outer feathers. Males are generally brighter than females and immature birds. The species has a fairly plain face compared with many other warblers and a stout, pointed bill. Its repeated, musical trill is often easier to notice than the bird itself, especially in tall pine trees.
value.rangeHabitat: Pine Warblers breed mainly in the southeastern United States, with a breeding range extending northward into parts of the eastern United States. They use mature pine stands, pine plantations, open pine woodland, and mixed forests containing abundant pines. In winter, many occur in the southeastern United States, the Caribbean, and nearby regions. In Costa Rica, the species is not a regular or expected migrant; it is known only from rare, exceptional records or vagrants, rather than an established wintering population.
value.migrationStatus: Mostly migratory in the northern and central parts of its range, with some birds resident in the southern United States. Costa Rica lies well south of its normal winter range, and Pine Warbler is considered a very rare vagrant there rather than a regular seasonal visitor.
value.breeding: Breeding usually occurs from spring into summer in mature pine trees. The female builds a small cup nest, commonly placed on a horizontal pine branch and made from plant fibers, bark, grasses, and other materials, with the exterior often decorated with lichens or similar material. The clutch commonly contains several eggs. The female performs most incubation, while both adults feed the nestlings and care for the fledglings.
value.dietFeeding: The Pine Warbler feeds on caterpillars, beetles, ants, grasshoppers, spiders, and other arthropods, especially during the breeding season. It also eats substantial amounts of seeds, including pine seeds, and may take fruit or berries. It usually searches among pine needles and branches but also descends to the ground, where it can walk or hop while feeding. This ground-foraging behavior helps distinguish it from many other tree-feeding warblers.
value.behavior: Pine Warblers are active but often unobtrusive birds. They commonly forage alone or in pairs and may join mixed-species flocks outside the breeding season. Their flight is typically short and direct between trees. Males defend territories with a persistent trilled song, often delivered from a high pine branch. The species frequently returns to the same pine-rich areas and may spend considerable time feeding on or near the ground.

conservation.populationTrend: The overall population is considered stable to increasing, although local numbers can vary with changes in pine habitat, forest management, and regional conditions.
